#### **1.  Introduction & Executive Summary** 

###### **1.1 Introduction** 

Since the release of our last 3-Year Silver Forecast on 1st December, silver has experienced a period of volatile trading, characterised by three broad phases. First, price action last December saw silver weaken in line with other precious metals, realising an intramonth fall of over $5, or 15%.  This partly reflected a less bullish outlook for the global economy (driven at the time by growing concerns over Europe’s prospects) which, with silver’s far greater exposure as an industrial metal, saw it experience a larger intra-month decline compared with gold’s 10% fall. 

Second, from its low point at end-2011 ($26.16 on 29th December, basis the London fix), silver rose markedly through to end-February (with January seeing the largest monthly gain in over four months). In

so doing, silver comfortably recouped December’s losses before going on, by the end of February, to post its highest price since 22nd September 2011. One of the key drivers of this rally was the change in investor sentiment, principally in the futures market. While December last year had seen net investor long positions on Comex fall markedly (to a ten-year low by end-2011), 2012 has, by contrast, witnessed a sharp reversal, with net investor long positions at endFebruary (their high point for 2012 to-date) realising a more than two-fold gain against end-2011. Third, early March saw investor liquidations emerge, which hint at the overnight price action (from a London perspective) of 29th February. The sharp price correction emerged in the wake of a Federal Reserve meeting where clarity as to a further round of quantitative easing had been expected. As the table above shows, we have scaled back our forecast for this year, with 2013-14 little changed from the November report.  To an extent, this reflects the difficulty silver has experienced in building on its strong January performance, a feature that was evident before the end-February sell-off.  Nevertheless, against the backdrop of an ongoing sovereign debt crisis and loose monetary policies, we expect underlying demand for silver as a safe haven asset to remain intact. 

Although we are still positive towards silver this year price volatility will remain elevated, which at times may deter investors from entering the silver market. This will owe much to growing concerns about the global economic outlook, while a firmer US dollar may also depress prices.  Although the United States has reported increasingly positive economic data, unemployment remains at elevated levels, while a struggling property market continues to impact economic growth.  Separately, fears have also grown of a more sustained economic slowdown in China, with the government targeting the lowest rate of GDP growth since the late 1990s.  In addition, European growth, already battered by the sovereign debt crisis, may well suffer further as European leaders push their southern neighbours in particular to adopt stricter austerity measures. 

As a result, stabilisation of the debt problem may only start to emerge during the second half of 2013. Although this will gradually reduce silver’s appeal as a safe haven the decline in investment is only likely to emerge towards the end of next year, given the reluctance of some monetary authorities to tighten policy, particularly in the United States.  Furthermore, the emergence of rising inflation, also in the United States will also help to limit the fall in silver prices. Moreover, even though economic conditions will eventually stabilise towards the end of 2013, we do not believe the initial weakness in prices will trigger heavy net liquidations.  As such, combined with a high starting point for 2013, we still expect silver to average $38.55 that year.  Even if the boom has proved bigger and more sustained than we previ

As a result, the silver price will need to clear at much lower levels and, with a lack of price sensitive silver demand, this means that far weaker prices are required in order for this to happen. In addition to the Base Case, we also offer two alternative scenarios for the global economy that are very different to our central forecast. In each instance, these have distinct implications for the level and trajectory of silver prices over the next three years. **Scenario B** (with a 40% probability) presents the most positive outlook for silver prices, with an investor-led bull market continuing throughout the entire forecast period. A key difference between Scenario B and the Base Case is that the former assumes that sovereign debt problems continue in 2013, rather than seeing the start of resolution this year. Meanwhile, the United States, faced with only a slowly improving economy, but more importantly still elevated levels of unemployment, may well postpone tightening fiscal policy, which will see the sovereign debt crisis move over to the United States and spread to Japan over the next two years. Against a backdrop of still loose fiscal and monetary polices, the world economy this year is expected to avoid a sharp slowdown, to the benefit of industrial metals. Furthermore, a more rapid increase in inflation seems increasingly likely, particularly in the United States where this is forecast to near 6% by 2014. This should prompt a move into silver by a broader group of institutional investors, which in turn will result in prices racing ahead to post an average of $60.15 in 2013, **6** 3-Year Silver Forecast - March 2012 **CONFIDENTIAL** while 2014 sees a more sedate improvement, of 9%, to a full year average of $65.40. A complete contrast is **Scenario C** (with a 15% probability), where investment demand is forecast to peak this year. While we could see an escalation

of the European debt crisis in the near term, pressure from the bond market may well force the region’s peripheral countries to speed up on austerity plans and restore investor confidence.  As more fiscal tightening measures take place, we expect that fears regarding the sovereign debt crisis will ease considerably.  Related to this is the fact that the commodity complex is likely to suffer (as a result of lower world GDP growth) under this scenario, which will then see inflation fears eventually subside.  These factors should reduce precious metals’ appeal to investors, most notably from mid-2012 onwards, when a marked reduction in investment results in prices slipping to levels that are more in line with silver’s underlying supply/demand fundamentals by 2014. 

Much of the above has focused on the principal economic variables and investment.  However, we do not subscribe to the view that price direction and level are determined by investment alone.  The following analysis of expected trends in the underlying supply/demand variables shows that these will also play an important, if subsidiary, role in silver price determination in 2012-14. 

###### **1.2 Base Case Scenario** 

On the supply side, global **mine production** is set to post successive record highs over 2012-2014, rising from 783 Moz in 2011 to 867 Moz in the final forecast year.  Growth averages 3% per annum over this period, due to a robust project pipeline, underpinned by a healthy performance from the base metals sector and further supported by healthy precious metal prices. Although primary silver mining and by-product base metal supply will improve over the forecast, the largest gains will emerge in by-product gold output.  This will see its share of global mine production rise from 13% in 2011 to 20% by 2014.  Since the last forecast, the global total has been adjusted marginally lower. 

**Scrap** supply, meanwhile, is set to follow a different path.  Volumes are expected to remain broadly flat this year (at around 235 Moz), although it is worth noting that the level is nonetheless historically high.  Supply remains elevated in 2013, before slumping to just over 203 Moz in 2014.  This decline is mostly due to steep price-led losses from jewellery and silverware, as well 









as ongoing declines from the photographic sector. Scrap this year has been revised lower from our last report (due to the cut in prices), while volumes in 2013 and 2014 have been raised, due to firmer expectations for jewellery and silverware recycling. 

With regard to **net producer hedging** , we expect some 25 Moz of supply from this source this year. Prolonged price strength in 2013 fosters another year of hedging, before lower prices in 2014 prompt a return to de-hedging.  Hedging volumes in 2012 and 2013 have been revised lower since the last report, on the back of our reduced price expectations. 

**Net government sales** will stay broadly flat this year, before dropping sharply in 2013 and r

eturning to net neutrality in 2014.  The series remains unchanged from the November report. 

Turning to global silver demand, total fabrication is set to climb by 4% between 2011 and 2014.  By far the largest component of this is **industrial** fabrication, which will reach successive record highs over the forecast.  Offtake this year rises by a modest 3%, as end-use demand struggles in an uncertain macroeconomic climate.  The latter two forecast years then each return growth of 5% as consumer spending begins to recover in a brightening economic climate, taking offtake in 2014 to just over 560 Moz, 13% higher compared with 2011.  Since the last forecast, the series has been revised lower primarily due to the downwards revision to last year’s total, which has produced a lower starting point. 

**Jewellery** fabrication is also expected to rise over the forecast period.  This in part will be driven by ongoing market penetration in the youth demographic and substitution gains at the expense of gold.  The fastest rate of growth (of 9%) emerges in 2014, as a result of falling prices, coupled with the impact of improved economic growth on consumer spending. **Silverware** , in contrast, will extend its long term trend of decline until 2013, before posting a modest price-led recovery in 2014, although the total remains historically low. **Photographic** demand is expected to maintain its downward trajectory, primarily as digital technology continues to erode silver halide’s market share. Finally, demand for **coins & medals** is set to realise further gains this year, to a new record of 138 Moz. Although volumes will start to wane thereafter, they will nonetheless remain at historically elevated levels.

Overall, the supply/demand forecast shows that the market will remain in surplus (as defined by the sum of mine production plus scrap less fabrication, excluding coins) until 2014.  This market surplus in the early years should be comfortably absorbed by investors whilst the economic backdrop remains uncertain. However, once this begins to improve, silver becomes vulnerable to a major correction as its supply/demand elements appear insufficiently price elastic to respond. This leaves the market still dependent on a body of investors to purchase both the fundamental surplus at ever lower prices and to absorb selling from other investors.  This outcome explains the persistence of implied net investment in the face of far weaker prices. 

###### **1.3 Alternative Scenarios** 

**Scenario B** offers the most bullish outcome for silver prices, with nominal silver prices almost doubling between 2011 and 2014.  This is driven by surging investor interest, underpinned by a highly inflationary backdrop and attendant dollar weakness.  World Investment peaks in 2014 at some $25 billion, almost six times higher compared with the Base Case. 

Under Scenario B, supply from all sources is n

otably higher compared with the Base Case, most notably from scrap and net producer hedging. Mine production also ramps up, adding over 100 Moz by 2014 (compared with the 2011 total). This sees total supply reach a peak of 1,201 Moz in 2014, 131 Moz higher than under the Base Case. Total fabrication, meanwhile, also shows stronger gains, led by more robust offtake in coins & medals, as a result of surging investor demand. In contrast, industrial offtake in 2014 is forecast to be broadly similar to that seen in 2014 under the Base Case. This is because higher silver prices accelerate the rate of substitution and thrifting, which outweigh gains driven by the faster pace of world GDP growth. Jewellery demand, meanwhile, sees a more subdued rate of increase under Scenario B (due to higher prices), while silverware and photographic offtake post comparatively steeper rates of decline. Since our last report, the most notable change has been to the mine supply series, which has been revised lower as we have moderated expectations for several projects. On the demand side, the outlook for industrial demand has also been paired back, largely due to the downward revision to the total 2011, which has resulted in a lower benchmark for the forecast series. **Scenario C** offers our most bearish outcome for silver prices, which fall to just $14.05 in 2014 (basis the annual average). This performance is due primarily to far weaker investor interest, as more aggressive fiscal tightening eases inflationary fears. The slow rate of economic growth this fosters also dampens investor demand for silver due to the lacklustre industrial outlook. Indeed, under this case, World Investment will have already peaked in 2011 at some $10 billion, after which it will collapse to $2.1 billion by 2014, less than half the level seen under the Base Case at this time. Price & Economic Assumptions** ###### **2.1 Introduction** Thomson Reuters GFMS’ views for the forecast period are presented in the form of three probability-weighted scenarios, namely the Base Case Scenario, Scenario B and Scenario C. Under our **Base Case** , we expect to see a slowdown in world GDP growth this year. This will mainly be driven by the ongoing sovereign debt crisis in Europe, fiscal policy tightening in places and a reduction in industrial production in major advanced economies. Although developing countries continue to expand, their growth is likely to moderate due to tight monetary conditions in a number of locations and downward pressure on external demand stemming from economic and financial problems in industrialised countries. Nevertheless, we expect the world economy to improve gradually over the final two years of our forecast. We view this as the most likely scenario, and have therefore assigned this with a 45% probability. Under our more bullish **Scenario B** , to which we assign a 40% probability, we expect a global economic recovery with higher growth rates in both the major advanced and developing countries over the forecast period. We assume that the US government and the Federal Reserve will continue to implement ultraloose monetary and fiscal policies, at least until late-2014. We therefore expect to see the dollar weaken and inflation rising during this period, with the latter reaching an annual average of 5.8% in 2014.
